drawdown.def: The fall in an account's value from its highest value so far to a later low, as a fraction of that peak.

maximum drawdown.def: The largest drawdown in a record: the worst peak-to-trough loss over the whole period.

conditional drawdown at risk.def: The average of the drawdowns beyond a chosen percentile, such as the worst 5% of them. It describes the tail of drawdowns rather than the single worst one.

leverage.def: The ratio of a position's total exposure to the capital behind it. An account holding 1.4 million dollars of an index on 1 million dollars of its own money has 1.4 times leverage.

margin.def: The capital a broker requires you to hold in the account to keep a position open. It acts as a deposit against losses.

margin call.def: A broker's demand for more money, or a smaller position, when the account's equity falls below its margin requirement.

forced liquidation.def: The broker's closing of your positions at market prices when you do not meet a margin call in time.

mark-to-market.def: Valuing a position at the current market price, with the gain or loss counted in the account each day whether or not the position is closed.

Reg-T margin.def: A margin model, named for the Federal Reserve's Regulation T, that requires a fixed percentage of each position's value. It is simple and does not change with market stress.

portfolio margin.def: A margin model that sets the requirement from the loss the whole portfolio would suffer in stress scenarios, such as a 15% index move with shifts in implied volatility. It allows more leverage in calm markets and can expand sharply in stress.

SOFR.def: The Secured Overnight Financing Rate, a benchmark US interest rate for borrowing cash overnight.

basis point.def: One hundredth of a percentage point, so 20 basis points is 0.20%. Abbreviated bp, plural bps.

box spread.def: A combination of four options whose value at expiry is fixed whatever the underlying does. Selling one is a way to borrow money at the interest rate implied by its price.

futures contract.def: An agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date. Only a deposit is paid up front, so a future gives exposure with leverage built in.

in-the-money.def: Said of an option that would pay something if exercised now: a call whose strike is below the underlying's price, or a put whose strike is above it.

embedded leverage.def: The leverage built into an option, where a small premium controls a large exposure. Buyers pay for it in the option's price, a cost called embedded leverage drag.

Greeks.def: The measures of how an option's value changes with the underlying's price, with time, with volatility and with interest rates: delta, gamma, theta, vega and rho.

assignment.def: What happens to the seller of an option when its holder exercises it: the seller must buy or sell the underlying, or pay the cash difference, at the strike.

implied volatility.def: The volatility that, put into an option pricing model, reproduces an option's market price. It is the market's price for future movement, quoted as an annualized percentage.

path dependency.def: The property of a strategy whose result depends on the route prices take and not only on where they end, for example because a margin call can close it along the way.

put spread.def: A position of two put options on the same underlying and expiry but with different strikes, one bought and one sold. Its gain or loss at expiry is capped by the distance between the strikes.

cash-secured put.def: A sold put option backed by enough cash to buy the underlying at the strike if it is assigned. Nothing is borrowed, so it cannot receive a margin call.

variance risk premium.def: The payment option sellers earn for taking the other side of investors who want to hedge volatility, seen as implied volatility above the volatility that follows, on average.

correlation.def: A number from minus 1 to plus 1 measuring how closely two series move together: their covariance divided by the product of their standard deviations.

covariance.def: The average product of two variables' deviations from their means. It is positive when they tend to move the same way and negative when they tend to move opposite ways.

Treasury bond.def: A bond issued by the US government through the Treasury.

covariance matrix.def: A square table holding each asset's variance on its diagonal and each pair's covariance off it. With the portfolio's weights, it gives the portfolio's variance.

tail correlation.def: Correlation measured only over extreme periods, such as the worst months for stocks. It can differ sharply from correlation measured over all periods.

betting against beta.def: A strategy that holds low-beta stocks against high-beta ones. Its premise is that investors unable to borrow bid up high-beta stocks to get more market exposure.

trend following.def: A strategy that buys assets whose own prices have been rising and sells those whose prices have been falling. Also called time-series momentum.

60/40 portfolio.def: A portfolio holding 60% of its value in stocks and 40% in bonds, rebalanced back to those weights from time to time.

out-of-the-money.def: Said of an option that would pay nothing if exercised now: a call whose strike is above the underlying's price, or a put whose strike is below it.

liquidity.def: The cost of getting into and out of a position: the bid-ask spread, the market impact of your own order, and how both widen under stress.

bid-ask spread.def: The gap between the highest price a buyer offers, the bid, and the lowest price a seller asks, the ask. Crossing it is the immediate cost of trading.

mid-quote.def: The price halfway between the bid and the ask, and the price at which academic backtests assume trades are filled.

market impact.def: The move in price that your own order causes, paid as a worse fill that grows with the size of the order.

backtest.def: A test of a trading rule on historical data, showing what the rule would have earned had it been followed.

signal.def: An observation that updates the probabilities of what a market will do, such as a volatility ratio crossing a level. On its own it is not tradable.

strategy.def: A rule that translates signals into trades: what to buy or sell, when, and when to get out.

allocation.def: How much capital, or how much of the portfolio's risk, each strategy is given.

VIX.def: Cboe's index of the implied volatility of S&P 500 options over the next 30 days.

quality factor.def: A portfolio tilt toward the stocks of profitable, financially sound companies.

carry trade.def: A position that earns the gap in yield between two assets, such as borrowing in a low-interest currency to lend in a high-interest one.

equity risk premium.def: The extra return that stocks are expected to pay over safe assets, as payment for bearing the risk that they fall when times are already bad.

options expiration.def: The date on which a series of listed options expires, abbreviated OPEX. The monthly SPX expiration falls on the third Friday of the month.

kill criterion.def: A rule, set in advance, for when to stop trading a strategy, such as a drawdown or a shortfall against its expected return beyond a stated limit.

risk premium.def: An expected return above the risk-free rate, paid to whoever bears a risk that others would pay to avoid.

arbitrage.def: A profit made without bearing risk, by exploiting a difference between prices that should agree.

term premium.def: The extra return expected from holding long-term bonds rather than rolling over short-term ones, as payment for bearing interest rate risk.

convenience yield.def: The benefit of holding a physical commodity rather than a contract to receive it later, such as being able to use it during a shortage.

limits to arbitrage.def: The costs, risks and capital constraints that stop rational traders from betting fully against a mispricing, so that it can persist.

post-earnings announcement drift.def: The tendency of a stock's price to keep moving in the direction of an earnings surprise for weeks after the announcement. Abbreviated PEAD.

momentum.def: The tendency of assets that have risen recently to keep rising, and of those that have fallen to keep falling. Cross-sectional momentum compares stocks with one another; time-series momentum compares each asset with its own past.

low-volatility anomaly.def: The pattern in which low-volatility, low-beta stocks earn more relative to their risk than high-volatility stocks, against the simple rule that more risk pays more.

beta.def: A measure of how much an asset moves with the market. A stock with a beta of 1.5 moves, on average, 1.5% for each 1% move in the market.

capacity.def: The amount of capital a strategy can absorb before its own trading erodes its edge.

order flow.def: The stream of buy and sell orders arriving at a market, and the imbalance between them.

market maker.def: A firm that stands ready to buy and sell, quoting both a bid and an ask, and hedges the risk it takes on. In options it is usually called the dealer.

adverse selection.def: The loss from trading with someone who knows more than you do, so that the trades you get are the ones that are bad for you.

gamma exposure.def: An estimate of the total gamma that dealers hold across all strikes, and so of how much hedging they must do as the index moves. Abbreviated GEX.

0DTE.def: Options with zero days to expiry: options traded on the day they expire.

pin risk.def: The risk, near expiry, that the underlying settles close to a strike, leaving it uncertain whether an option is exercised.

sleeve.def: The part of a portfolio given to one strategy, with its own capital or risk budget.
